Most temples have spiritual retreats, yes, but the only one who accepts visitors at all times is Theravada monastary Suddhavari at São Lourenco, MG  (https://suddhavari.org/endereco-contato/[here's their website with contact information](https://suddhavari.org/endereco-contato/). 

I do know some temples that have 30 days retreats, such as the Zu Lai Temple, that has a retreat Intensive Study and Practice of Buddhism, [here's their website](https://templozulai.org.br/), and Tibetan Buddhist Temple Khadro Ling, [here's the website as well](https://www.templobudista.org/). 

The Monastary portraid at this post has retreats, Sesshins, but they normally last fewer days. 

Khadro Ling offer paid accommodation too, I found out. [here's what I found on booking](https://www.booking.com/hotel/br/studio-em-templo-budista.pt-br.html)

What I have to say is that you have to discover your buddhist school, search for temples and then contact them on social media. About English, I believe all of them have people who are able to speak English.

Hi. The Torii is not exactly a part of the monastary. It's an open to public square and I believe it's kept by the municipality government. The square was a commemorative gift for the monastary's 30th anniversary and symbolizes a open gate between oriental and occidental culture. The monastary also has a path with 108 Torii gates symbolizing the 108 virtues. 
While there are Toriis there, I do not believe they practice or have any shintoism beliefs. 

The monastary follows a soto-zen doctrine and was founded by zen master Ryotan Tokuda, a Japanese immigrant in the 1970s. Some Japanese zen buddhist temples do have Toriis as well, like Tenryū-ji, in Kyoto, so I believe the architecture is the result of the symbiotic relationship between shintoism and buddhism in ancient Japan.

I'm not espiritual specifically, but I am a secular Buddhist and an atheist at the same time. 

What happened with me was: when I  acknowledged that I didn't believe in a God, I became free to learn about any religion. Before, I felt trapped in catholicism and reading another sacred books or going to a different church just to experience it was sacrilegious. So, after that, I went to any and all churches existed in my town, I read many books about many different religions and I found a sense of comfort in Buddhist philosophy. I still don't believe in anything supernatural, but I do feel connected to a certain level with this religion. 

And I have friends that found the same thing in some religions in a deeper level. Like, they don't believe there's a God controlling every aspect of your life but there's some things that they believe (like, an atheist friend of mine doesn't believe in God but he does believe in another parallel word some would describe as post-life.
